styles.name: Radiant Fire
styles.blurb: Heat that arrives before you do — you decide fast, commit out loud, and the room either warms to you or gets out of the way.

palette.line: Solar amber is your everyday register, signal red is what you reach for when you need the room to turn, and ash basalt is the weight that stops the whole thing burning out by Thursday.

A brass key kept in the coat you wear most
palette.lucky_days: Tuesday and Sunday — the first for starting things, the second for finishing them.

mistake_one.title: You mistake speed for certainty
mistake_one.body: The thing you are strongest at — moving before the room has finished thinking — is also the thing that costs you most. A fire-and-sun profile reads its own momentum as evidence: because the decision came quickly, it feels like it came from somewhere deep. Often it did. Sometimes it came from nothing more than the discomfort of sitting still, and the two feel identical from the inside.
mistake_one.fix: Give any decision you can explain in under ten seconds one night before you act on it. Not a week — a night. If it is still obvious in the morning it was conviction; if it has gone quiet it was restlessness wearing conviction's coat.

styles.name: Deep Water
styles.blurb: Everything registers and almost nothing shows — you read a room in seconds and give it back slowly, on your own terms.

palette.line: Midnight indigo is where you are most yourself, moon silver is what lets other people find you in it, and deep violet is the accent to use once in a room and never twice.
talismans: Moonstone — worn where you can reach it without looking
Labradorite — kept on the desk rather than on the body
A small dish of sea salt by the door you use
palette.lucky_days: Monday and Thursday — Monday for reading a situation, Thursday for saying it out loud.

mistake_one.title: You wait for the perfect moment to say it
mistake_one.body: You take in more than anyone around you and hold it longer, which is why your read on a situation is almost always right. It is also why it arrives late. A water-and-moon profile trusts timing the way other people trust logic, and it will hold a true and useful thing for weeks waiting for a moment clean enough to deserve it. The moment rarely comes, the thing goes unsaid, and the situation resolves without you in it.
mistake_one.fix: Set a ceiling instead of a moment. Three days from noticing something to naming it, clumsy wording included. The awkward version said on Tuesday does more work than the perfect version you never quite reach.

styles.name: Grounded Earth
styles.blurb: Weight and patience — you build things that stay built, and the value of that stays invisible until the day it isn't.

palette.line: Moss green and quarry stone are the two you can put anything against, warm clay is what stops the pair going austere, and bark umber belongs on the edges rather than the field.
talismans: Smoky quartz — in the pocket you actually use
Jasper — kept where you work, not where you rest
An unglazed clay bead on a plain cord
palette.lucky_days: Friday and Saturday — Friday to settle things, Saturday to begin them.

mistake_one.title: You absorb the cost instead of naming it
mistake_one.body: Steadiness is the thing everyone around you relies on, and you deliver it so reliably that the delivery stops being visible. An earth-and-calm profile takes the extra hour, the awkward conversation, the thing nobody else picked up — and takes it quietly enough that no one ever learns it was extra. Over a few years the baseline moves. What you once took on as a favour is now simply what you do.
mistake_one.fix: Say the cost out loud once, at the moment it happens, without asking for anything in return. Not a complaint and not a negotiation — one sentence naming what it took. People adjust to information far more readily than they adjust to resentment.

mistake_one.title: You leave at the exact moment it gets valuable
mistake_one.body: You see the shape of a thing before anyone else does, and the seeing is genuinely the hard part — an air-and-sun profile turns out more usable ideas in a month than most people have in a year. But the interest is front-loaded. Once the shape is clear the rest reads as admin, so you move on, the idea belongs to whoever stayed, and you are left with the accurate and useless memory of having thought of it first.
mistake_one.fix: Pick one thing a quarter and stay past the point where it stops being interesting. Not everything — one. The boredom is not a signal that the work is finished; it is the toll on the stretch where the value actually gets collected.
